originalIllustrations.prompt:
Create a polished ORIGINAL illustrated nursing-study infographic, portrait 1024x1536. Deep sapphire, emerald, amethyst and burgundy jewel tones with thin antique gold borders and restrained Klimt-inspired abstract medical mosaic corner decorations. Large crisp cream text, strong hierarchy, generous spacing; medical illustrations and a memorable scene, not a wall of text. No company logos. Title: "GASTRIC vs DUODENAL ULCERS". Subtitle: "Time the pain — watch for bleeding in BOTH".
Top third: a clear anatomically plausible cutaway of distal esophagus entering a stomach and then the short C-shaped duodenum connected through the pylorus. The stomach is on the viewer's right as in an anterior human anatomy view; duodenum on viewer's left. Mark a small crater confined to the stomach mucosa as "Gastric: stomach" and a small crater in the proximal duodenum as "Duodenal: first small-intestine segment". Do not show a full-thickness hole or leaking contents. No need to depict the whole abdomen.
Middle: two evenly sized large comparison panels. LEFT burgundy panel heading "GASTRIC". Illustration: a person at a dinner table with the first plate of food, hand over upper abdomen, a small stomach-shaped character rings an early dinner bell. Text: "Food often worsens pain"; "Soon after a meal"; mnemonic on gold plaque: "G = Grief with food". RIGHT emerald panel heading "DUODENAL". Illustration: another diner gets brief comfort from a meal, then a clearly labeled clock "2–3 hours later" and a moon cue signal returning upper-abdominal pain. Text: "Food may briefly relieve pain"; "Pain returns later or at night"; mnemonic: "D = Delayed discomfort". Each cue is beside its associated clinical fact. Small caveat between panels and lower strip: "Typical study patterns — symptoms overlap."
Bottom third: shared alert strip with blood-drop icon, BP cuff, pulse and blood-test tube icons and black tarry stool icon, tasteful no gore. Heading "BOTH CAN BLEED". Large readable lines: "BP may fall • Pulse may rise"; "Black, tarry stool or bloody vomit"; "Hemoglobin may fall". Small supporting line: "These signs do NOT identify the ulcer's location."
Distinct highlighted nurse priority box: "PRIORITY: Assess bleeding or shock urgently." Second line: "Sudden severe pain + rigid abdomen: suspect perforation."
Footer: "H. pylori and NSAIDs: common causes of BOTH." Final small line "Original Study Hub memory illustration • Patterns are not a diagnosis".
All text must be readable, spelled correctly, no extra invented facts, no brand watermark. Preserve natural human anatomy and make the pain-timing contrast visually obvious.

originalIllustrations.prompt: Create an original, clinically careful, illustrated nursing teaching poster. Portrait 1024x1536. Deep sapphire and emerald backgrounds, burgundy and amethyst panel accents, restrained Klimt-inspired gold mosaic border, cream legible text. Rich anatomical illustrations, generous space, minimal text, large labels with exact leader lines. No logo. No patient photograph simulation: footer clearly 'Original Study Hub anatomical illustration • Not a patient image'. Title "UPPER GI: SEE THE STRUCTURES". Four clear labeled panels. 1 "STOMACH LANDMARKS": large anatomical cutaway stomach attached to esophagus and C-shaped duodenum, anatomically accurate anterior view. Label Cardia (entry), Fundus (upper dome), Body (middle), Antrum (distal portion), Pylorus (exit), Rugae (internal folds), Duodenum. Correct orientation: stomach body toward viewer right and duodenal C curve viewer left. 2 "REFLUX vs HIATAL HERNIA": two small side-by-side anatomical views. Reflux: stomach stays BELOW diaphragm; upward arrow from stomach through weak lower esophageal sphincter. Sliding hiatal hernia: gastroesophageal junction and upper stomach rise ABOVE diaphragm through esophageal hiatus. Clearly label diaphragm and junction. 3 "BARRETT'S CHANGE": circular illustrated lumen comparison: normal pale pink smooth esophageal mucosa versus tongues of salmon-colored mucosa extending up from the gastroesophageal junction. Text "Biopsy confirms the cell change." Label "Illustrated endoscopic appearance". No fake histology claims. 4 "GASTRITIS vs ULCER": two enlarged lining cutaways: gastritis is inflamed irritated surface without a deep crater; ulcer is focal deeper crater in mucosa, NOT a hole through entire wall. Text "Inflamed lining" versus "Deeper focal defect". At bottom gold memory strip "Gate • Dome • Body • Grinder • Exit" with mappings "Cardia • Fundus • Body • Antrum • Pylorus". No other clinical advice.

originalIllustrations.label: Original Study Hub teaching illustration, not a clinical photograph
originalIllustrations.prompt: Create an original, clinically careful, illustrated nursing teaching poster. Portrait 1024x1536. Deep sapphire and emerald backgrounds, burgundy and amethyst panel accents, restrained Klimt-inspired gold mosaic border, cream legible text. Rich anatomical illustrations, generous space, minimal text, large labels with exact leader lines. No logo. No patient photograph simulation: footer clearly 'Original Study Hub anatomical illustration • Not a patient image'. Title "BOWEL PROBLEMS: WHAT CHANGES?". Four large anatomically detailed panels with restrained non-gory tissue illustration. Panel1 "MECHANICAL OBSTRUCTION": a bowel tube with an adhesion band compressing one point; dilated bowel and fluid above blockage, decompressed bowel below. Label "Physical blockage", "Dilated upstream". Panel2 "ILEUS": a set of diffusely distended bowel loops, no single blockage, gentle crossed-out peristalsis arrows. Label "Movement slows or stops", "No mechanical blockage". Panel3 "VOLVULUS": clearly demonstrate one bowel loop twisting with its mesentery around its attachment, narrowing both inflow/outflow. Label "Twist", "Blood flow can be threatened". Panel4 "INTUSSUSCEPTION": one segment of bowel telescoping INSIDE the adjacent receiving segment, cutaway shows concentric layers; optional small transverse target-ring inset explicitly "Cross-section". Label "Telescopes", "Target-like layers". Gold mnemonic strip: "BLOCK • STOP • TWIST • TELESCOPE". Red priority strip "Severe pain, vomiting, distention or worsening condition: urgent assessment." Small line "Bowel sounds alone do not distinguish these conditions." Do not depict these illustrations as X-rays or CT scans.

originalIllustrations.label: Original Study Hub teaching illustration, not a clinical photograph
originalIllustrations.prompt: Create an original, clinically careful, illustrated nursing teaching poster. Portrait 1024x1536. Deep sapphire and emerald backgrounds, burgundy and amethyst panel accents, restrained Klimt-inspired gold mosaic border, cream legible text. Rich anatomical illustrations, generous space, minimal text, large labels with exact leader lines. No logo. No patient photograph simulation: footer clearly 'Original Study Hub anatomical illustration • Not a patient image'. Title "ABDOMEN: WHERE AM I LOOKING?". Upper two-thirds a large front-view torso with a 3-by-3 grid correctly aligned on the abdomen, not on the chest. Label patient's RIGHT over viewer LEFT and patient's LEFT over viewer RIGHT. Nine regions readable in exact grid: top row viewer left "Right hypochondriac", center "Epigastric", viewer right "Left hypochondriac"; middle row "Right lumbar", "Umbilical", "Left lumbar"; bottom row "Right iliac", "Hypogastric", "Left iliac". Under grid add three concise memory lines "Top: liver • stomach • spleen" / "Middle: flanks • navel" / "Bottom: appendix side • bladder area • sigmoid side". These are broad location aids, not organ boundaries. Lower third two rich clinical illustrations of torso skin on different skin tones. Left front-view umbilicus with irregular purple-yellow ecchymosis centered around the NAVEL, label "CULLEN SIGN" and "Periumbilical bruising". Right side view torso with bruise over lateral FLANK between ribs and iliac crest, label "GREY TURNER SIGN" and "Flank bruising". No bruises on limbs. Footer redbox "These findings can suggest internal bleeding; they are not specific to pancreatitis." Anatomical educational illustration, not diagnosis.
